newsitem.title: USA: Merger trend in sugar industry sweetens profits.
newsitem.headline: Merger trend in sugar industry sweetens profits.

text.p: The merger this week between cane grower U.S. Sugar Corp and marketing firm United Sugars Corp is the latest marriage of opposite sectors of the industry, analysts said.
"The business is shrinking," Merrill Lynch sugar broker Peter Perez, said. "Factories are very old and costly to run and competition is too great so everybody is getting together to cut expenses."
Tuesday, U.S. Sugar Corp, one of Florida's largest sugarcane growers, said it joined United Sugars Corp, a marketing and distribution alliance made up of three Midwestern sugar beet cooperatives.

The union of sugar refiner Savannah Foods & Industries with privately-held producer Florida Crystals Inc in mid-July created the first U.S. sugar company with operations in growing, milling and refining of sugar.

Traditionally, the industry was divided into the cane growers based in Florida, Louisiana and Hawaii, and the beet producers of the Midwest and California. Refineries and mills also stood on opposite sides of the fence.
The 1988 purchase of U.S. cane refiner Amstar Corp, owner of Domino Sugar, by U.K.-based Tate & Lyle Plc, changed the face of the industry.

"All of a sudden there is more vertical integration where refineries are now picking up mills and beet refineries picking up some of the traditional cane users," Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes, said.

Analysts said the need for cost efficiencies, for supply security, for greater profitability, and the need to acquire an edge on the competition have all driven the trend. While independent producers still exist, they are finding it increasingly difficult to make a profit due to the cost structure and intensity of the industry.

"It's a question of people feeling that it's more efficient and a way to beat the competition, and if the competition is doing it, you've got to, too." Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson, said.
Analysts would not speculate on which companies are likely to merge next but agreed that consolidation within the industry will continue.
One industry source said cane producers in Louisiana, who have remained independent for the most part, could be the next takeover targets.
"We could have Louisiana follow the same path as Florida where growers get into the refined business," he said. "The key trend is vertical integration between raw sugar producers and refiners."
